name: Plant Systems
what: Covers the classification of vascular and non-vascular plants, the structure and function of root and shoot systems, specialised cells of the xylem, the mechanism of transpiration, and the factors affecting transpiration rate.
why: Plant systems provide a non-animal context for the same organisational principles covered in the mammalian systems, and transpiration is an important model of passive transport driven by concentration gradients and physical properties of water.

items.title: I can define vascular and non-vascular plants and explain how this classification relates to their size and habitat
items.what: Vascular plants have specialised conducting tissue (xylem and phloem) for transporting water and nutrients. Non-vascular plants lack this tissue, so they rely on osmosis and diffusion, restricting them to small sizes and moist environments.
items.why: This classification establishes the structural basis for all subsequent plant transport content and is directly tested in questions asking students to justify size differences between plant groups.
items.example: A moss (non-vascular) can grow only a few centimetres tall because water moves cell-to-cell by osmosis. A mountain ash (vascular) can reach 99.6 m because xylem transports water from roots to canopy over that entire distance.

items.title: I can describe the root system and shoot system of a vascular plant and the function of each organ within them
items.what: The root system (roots) absorbs water and minerals, anchors the plant and stores food. The shoot system (stems and leaves) supports the plant, transports substances and carries out photosynthesis.
items.why: Knowing the systems and their organs is the plant equivalent of knowing mammalian body systems and is required for full marks on questions comparing animal and plant organisation.
items.example: Secondary roots branch laterally from the primary root, greatly increasing total surface area for water absorption — analogous to the role of villi and microvilli in the mammalian small intestine.

items.title: I can explain how the structure of root hair cells is specialised for water and mineral uptake
items.what: Root hair cells are elongated thin projections from the root epidermis that extend between soil particles. Their shape maximises surface area for osmotic water uptake and active transport of mineral ions, without increasing the volume of the root.
items.why: Root hair cells are a named example in the study design of structure-function relationships in plant cells and are a direct parallel to intestinal epithelial cells in the mammalian digestive system.
items.example: A single rye plant has been estimated to have over 14 billion root hair cells with a combined surface area of approximately 400 m² — comparable to the absorptive surface of the human small intestine.

items.title: I can describe the composition, arrangement and role of xylem tissue in vascular transport
items.what: Xylem consists of two dead cell types — vessel elements (open-ended cylinders) and tracheids (tapered, overlapping cells) — both lignified for strength. They form continuous hollow tubes from root to leaf for unidirectional upward water transport.
items.why: Xylem structure is a named study design requirement and demonstrates how dead cells can still perform a vital structural and transport function.
items.example: In a cross-section of a woody stem, the rings visible to the naked eye are annual layers of xylem. Each ring represents one year's growth, and the wood itself is composed entirely of lignified xylem cell walls.

items.title: I can distinguish between vessel elements and tracheids in terms of structure and water movement
items.what: Vessel elements are wider, cylindrical and open at both ends, allowing unrestricted water flow. Tracheids are narrower, taper at both ends and overlap, with water moving laterally through pits between cells. Both are lignified and dead at maturity.
items.why: This distinction is a specific study design requirement and is tested in diagram interpretation questions comparing the two cell types.
items.example: Angiosperms (flowering plants) have both vessel elements and tracheids; gymnosperms (conifers) rely primarily on tracheids. The presence of vessel elements in angiosperms is associated with more efficient water transport at higher flow rates.

items.title: I can explain the cause and role of transpiration and how the cohesion-tension mechanism drives water movement through the xylem
items.what: Transpiration is the evaporation of water from leaves through open stomata. This creates a negative pressure (tension) in the xylem, pulling water upward. Cohesion between water molecules and adhesion to xylem walls maintain a continuous water column.
items.why: Transpiration is the primary mechanism of water transport in tall plants and is a key passive transport example — it requires no ATP from the plant yet moves water over 100 m vertically.
items.example: In a California redwood at 115 m, the tension generated by transpiration at the canopy is sufficient to pull a continuous water column from roots to leaves. Cohesion stops the column from breaking under this tension.

items.title: I can explain the role of stomata and guard cells in regulating transpiration
items.what: Stomata are pores bordered by two guard cells. When guard cells are turgid (water-filled), the stoma opens; when they are flaccid, it closes. Opening allows CO₂ entry for photosynthesis but also increases water loss by transpiration.
items.why: Guard cell function is a direct application of osmosis to plant physiology and illustrates the balance plants must maintain between photosynthesis and water conservation.
items.example: On a hot dry day, guard cells lose water to surrounding cells by osmosis, becoming flaccid and closing the stomata. This reduces transpiration water loss but simultaneously limits CO₂ uptake and slows photosynthesis.

items.title: I can explain how light intensity, temperature, wind and humidity affect the rate of transpiration
items.what: Transpiration rate increases with higher light intensity (stomata open wider), higher temperature (faster kinetic energy and evaporation), and greater wind speed (removes water vapour, steepening the concentration gradient). High humidity decreases transpiration by reducing the concentration gradient between leaf and air.
items.why: Environmental factors affecting transpiration are explicitly listed in the study design and are tested in experimental design and data interpretation questions.
items.example: A potted plant in a sealed transparent container will show little mass loss because the enclosed humid air reaches saturation and the concentration gradient between stomata and air falls to near zero, effectively halting transpiration.
